label: Review of Lie Groups
notes: This appendix, printed pages 407 through 427, condenses the Lie theory the main text relies on. We meet groups that are also smooth manifolds, their Lie algebras of left-invariant fields, the exponential map, smooth actions, homogeneous spaces, the adjoint representation, and bi-invariant metrics.

label: Lie Groups
notes: A Lie group fuses algebra and geometry: the multiplication and inversion maps are smooth, so the group operations are differentiable. Left translation is a diffeomorphism for every fixed element, which lets us transport tangent data from the identity across the whole manifold without distortion.

label: Left-Invariant Fields and the Lie Algebra
notes: A vector field is left-invariant when each left translation pushes it to itself. Evaluation at the identity gives a vector-space isomorphism between left-invariant fields and the tangent space there, and the bracket of two such fields is again left-invariant, making the tangent space a Lie algebra.

label: One-Parameter Subgroups
notes: A one-parameter subgroup is a smooth homomorphism from the additive real line into the group. Each is the integral curve through the identity of a unique left-invariant field, so its velocity at zero recovers the generating Lie algebra element. The flow is complete, defined for all real times.

label: The Exponential Map
notes: The exponential sends a Lie algebra vector to the time-one value of its one-parameter subgroup. It is a smooth map whose differential at the origin is the identity, hence a diffeomorphism near zero. For matrix groups it coincides with the familiar power-series matrix exponential.

label: Lie Group Homomorphisms
notes: A Lie group homomorphism is a smooth map respecting multiplication. Its differential at the identity is a Lie algebra homomorphism, and exponentials intertwine the two maps. This induced-map principle reduces questions about curved group maps to linear algebra on the tangent spaces at the identities.

label: Group Actions
notes: A smooth action lets a group move the points of a manifold. We track four properties: transitive when one orbit fills the space, free when only the identity fixes any point, and proper when the action-with-projection map is proper. These conditions control the quotient geometry.

label: Orbits and Isotropy
notes: The orbit of a point is everywhere it can be sent; its isotropy subgroup is everything fixing it. The orbit is the image of the group modulo the isotropy subgroup. Conjugate points have conjugate isotropy groups, so orbits of a transitive action all look the same.

label: Homogeneous Spaces
notes: When a Lie group acts smoothly, transitively, and properly, the quotient by an isotropy subgroup is a smooth manifold and the action map is a diffeomorphism onto it. Such homogeneous spaces are the model geometries: spheres, projective spaces, and hyperbolic space all arise this way.

label: The Adjoint Representation
notes: Conjugation by a group element fixes the identity, so its differential acts on the Lie algebra; this is the adjoint representation. Differentiating the adjoint at the identity yields the little-adjoint, which is exactly the Lie bracket. These representations encode how the group acts on its own infinitesimal symmetries.

label: Bi-Invariant Metrics
notes: A bi-invariant metric is invariant under both left and right translations. It exists on every compact Lie group and makes the adjoint maps isometries of the Lie algebra. Its geodesics through the identity are exactly the one-parameter subgroups, tying curvature directly to the bracket structure.

label: Synthesis
notes: From pages 407 to 427 a single dictionary emerges: groups linearize to algebras, the exponential reconnects them, actions build homogeneous spaces, and the adjoint plus a bi-invariant metric turn algebraic structure into Riemannian geometry. Keep this map handy whenever symmetry organizes a manifold in the main text.
